C0.quote: produce a concise slate of statements that proportionally represents the full spectrum
C0.note: Committee-election-like selection of statements with proportionality guarantees via queries to agents' utilities; treated as a voting procedure.

C1.quote: we achieve an approximate version of BJR adapted to the cost setting
C1.note: Main results are approximate cBJR guarantees and lower bounds (axiomatic); synthetic simulations; experiments on real review data with LLM-simulated utilities.

C2.1.value: utility functions (queried via discriminative query); no ballots named
C2.1.quote: each agent i ∈ N has a utility function ui

C2.2.quote: mapping each statement α ∈ U to one of r possible utility values
C2.2.note: Cardinal utility levels on r-point scale accessed through queries; input to PROSE is unstructured text about each user.

C2.3.quote: each agent i ∈ N has a utility function ui

C2.4.note: Algorithm applies directly to (predicted) utilities via queries; no submission/reporting is discussed.

C3.2.note: No statement that voters submit their held attitude.

C4.1.note: Input format is cardinal (CARD) or text; no ordinal/approval/dichotomous input in C2.2 codes.

C4.2.note: Term dichotomous preferences is not used.

C5.1.note: cBJR proportionality and agent utility used as evaluation criteria.

C5.2.quote: treat them as the true, underlying utilities
C5.2.note: Evaluated against utilities defined separately and accessed via queries (CoT utilities as proxy for true utilities).

VOT.note: Agents are passive; their utilities are queried; they take no action.

ORG.note: The designer's algorithm is the object of study, not a modelled agent.

DES.note: Designer's objective is not modelled as a choice.

claims.quote: demonstrating its effectiveness in generating representative slates from unstructured user opinions
provides a compelling vision for how AI can support democratic innovation

C9.2.note: Claims about user satisfaction/representation of real opinions need LLM-predicted utilities to match true utilities (partly stated as proxy, validated in E.5), and that real participants' held opinions are what is reflected; no statement on sincerity of submitted text.
